blocks.p: But let us return to our story. When the captains had gone back from the gate and come into the camp again, they called a council of war to consider what they should do next. Some said, “Let’s go up at once and fall on the town.” But most thought it better to send another summons to yield, because, as far as could be seen, Mansoul was now more inclined to yield than before. “And if,” they said, “while some of them are leaning our way, we put them off by harshness, we may drive them further from accepting our summons than we would want.” So they agreed to this advice. They called a trumpeter, put words into his mouth, set him his time, and wished him Godspeed. Within a few hours the trumpeter set out. Coming up to the wall, he made his way to Ear-gate and sounded there as he had been commanded. Those inside came out to see what was the matter, and the trumpeter made them this speech:

“O hard-hearted and pitiable town of Mansoul, how long will you love your sinful, sinful simplicity, and you fools delight in your scorning? Do you still despise the offers of peace and deliverance? Will you still refuse the golden offers of Shaddai, and trust the lies and falsehoods of Diabolus? When Shaddai has conquered you, do you think the memory of how you have behaved toward him will bring you peace and comfort? Or that by blustering language you can make him afraid, like a grasshopper? Does he plead with you because he fears you? Do you think you are stronger than he is? Look to the heavens, and see; consider the stars, how high they are. Can you stop the sun from running his course, or keep the moon from giving her light? Can you count the number of the stars, or stop the waterskins of heaven from pouring? Can you call for the waters of the sea and make them cover the face of the ground? Can you look on everyone who is proud and bring him low, and bind their faces in secret? Yet these are some of the works of our King, in whose name we come up to you today, so that you may be brought under his authority. In his name, therefore, I summon you again to surrender yourselves to his captains.”
At this summons the Mansoulians were at a loss for an answer. So Diabolus appeared at once and took it upon himself to reply, though he turned his speech to the people of Mansoul.

“Gentlemen,” he said, “and my faithful subjects: if what this summoner has said about the greatness of their King is true, his terror will keep you in bondage forever and make you creep and cringe. Why, how can you bear even now, while he is far off, to think of such a mighty one? And if you cannot bear to think of him at a distance, how could you bear to stand in his presence? I, your prince, am familiar with you, and you may play with me as you would with a grasshopper. Consider, then, what is to your advantage, and remember the freedoms I have granted you.

“Further, if everything this man has said is true, how does it come about that the subjects of Shaddai are so enslaved wherever they go? No one in the universe is so unhappy as they are, no one so trampled on.

“Consider, my Mansoul. I wish you were as unwilling to leave me as I am to leave you. But consider, I say: the ball is still at your foot. You have liberty, if you know how to use it; yes, and you have a king too, if you know how to love and obey him.”

At this speech the town of Mansoul hardened their hearts still more against the captains of Shaddai. The thought of his greatness quite crushed them, and the thought of his holiness sank them in despair. So after a short consultation they (and it was the Diabolonian party that did it) sent back word by the trumpeter that they were resolved to stick to their king and never yield to Shaddai, so it was useless to summon them further; they would rather die on the spot than yield. And now things seemed to have gone quite backward, and Mansoul seemed out of reach or call. Yet the captains, who knew what their Lord could do, would not yet be beaten out of heart. So they sent another summons, sharper and more severe than the last; but the more often they were called to be reconciled to Shaddai, the further off they went. “As they called them, so they went from them; yes, though they called them to the Most High.” [Hos. 11:2, 7]

So the captains gave up dealing with them in that way and began to think of another. They gathered together to confer freely among themselves about what more could be done to win the town and deliver it from the tyranny of Diabolus. One said this, and another that. Then the right noble Captain Conviction stood up and said, “My brothers, my opinion is this.

“First, that we keep our slings playing into the town continually, and keep it in constant alarm, harassing them day and night. By doing this we shall check the growth of their rampant spirit; for even a lion may be tamed by constant harassment.

“Second, this done, I advise that we next, with one consent, draw up a petition to our Lord Shaddai. In it, after we have shown our King the condition of Mansoul and of affairs here, and begged his pardon for our poor success, we will earnestly implore his Majesty’s help: that he will be pleased to send us more force and power, and some gallant and well-spoken commander to lead them, so that his Majesty may not lose the benefit of these good beginnings of his, but may complete his conquest of the town of Mansoul.”

To this speech of the noble Captain Conviction they all consented as one man, and agreed that a petition should be drawn up at once and sent with speed to Shaddai by a fit messenger. The petition read as follows:
Most gracious and glorious King, Lord of the best world, and Builder of the town of Mansoul:

At your command, dread Sovereign, we have put our lives in danger, and at your bidding we have made war on the famous town of Mansoul. When we went up against it, we first offered it conditions of peace, as our commission directed. But they, great King, made light of our counsel and would have none of our rebuke. They were for shutting their gates and keeping us out of the town. They also mounted their guns and sallied out against us, and have done us all the damage they could. But we have pursued them with alarm upon alarm, repaying them as they deserved, and have done some damage to the town.
Diabolus, Incredulity, and Willbewill are the chief workers against us. We are now in our winter quarters, but in such a way that we still harass and distress the town with a strong hand.

Once, as we believe, if we had had even one solid friend in the town, someone who would have backed the sound of our summons as they should have, the people might have yielded. But there was no one there but enemies, and no one to speak to the town on our Lord’s behalf. So although we have done what we could, Mansoul remains in a state of rebellion against you.

Now, King of kings, may it please you to pardon the failure of your servants, who have made no better progress in so desirable a work as the conquest of Mansoul. And send, Lord, as we now ask, more forces to Mansoul, so that it may be subdued; and a man to lead them, whom the town may both love and fear.

We do not say this because we are willing to give up the war (for we are ready to lay our bones before the place), but so that the town of Mansoul may be won for your Majesty. We also pray your Majesty to make haste in this matter, so that after its conquest we may be free to be sent on your other gracious errands. Amen.
The petition, drawn up in this way, was sent off in haste to the King by the hand of that good man, Mr. Love-to-Mansoul.

When this petition came to the King’s palace, to whom should it be delivered but to the King’s Son? He took it and read it, and because its contents pleased him well, he amended it and added to it in places with his own hand. Then he carried it in to the King; and when he had delivered it with a bow, he spoke for it himself, with all his authority.

Now the King was glad at the sight of the petition; but how much more, do you think, when it was seconded by his Son! It pleased him also to hear that his servants encamped against Mansoul were so wholehearted in the work and so steadfast in their resolve, and that they had already gained some ground against Mansoul.

So the King called Emmanuel his Son to him, who said, “Here I am, my Father.” Then the King said, “You know, as well as I do, the condition of the town of Mansoul, and what we have purposed, and what you have done to redeem it. Come now, therefore, my Son, and prepare yourself for the war, for you shall go to my camp at Mansoul. And there you shall prosper and prevail, and conquer the town of Mansoul.”

Then the King’s Son said, “Your law is within my heart; I delight to do your will. [Ps. 40:8] This is the day I have longed for, and the work I have waited for all this while. Grant me, therefore, whatever force you in your wisdom think fit, and I will go and deliver your perishing town of Mansoul from Diabolus and from his power. My heart has often been pained within me for the miserable town of Mansoul; but now it rejoices, now it is glad.”

And with that he leaped over the mountains for joy, saying, “I have not thought anything in my heart too dear for Mansoul. The day of vengeance is in my heart for you, my Mansoul [Isa. 63:4]; and I am glad that you, my Father, have made me the Captain of their salvation. [Heb. 2:10] And now I will begin to plague all those who have been a plague to my town of Mansoul, and I will deliver it from their hand.”

What the King’s Son had said to his Father flew like lightning all around the court, and what Emmanuel was going to do for the famous town of Mansoul became the only talk there. And you cannot imagine how taken the courtiers were with this design of the Prince. They were so moved by this work, and by the justice of the war, that the highest lord and greatest peer of the kingdom longed for a commission under Emmanuel, to help recover the miserable town of Mansoul for Shaddai.

Then it was decided that some should go and carry word to the camp that Emmanuel was coming to recover Mansoul, and that he would bring with him so mighty, so unbreakable a force that he could not be resisted. But oh, how ready the high ones at court were to run like errand boys to carry this news to the camp at Mansoul! Now when the captains learned that the King would send Emmanuel his Son, and that the Son delighted to be sent on this errand, they too, to show their pleasure at the thought of his coming, gave a shout that split the earth with the sound of it. Yes, the mountains answered back with the echo, and Diabolus himself tottered and shook.

For you must know that though Mansoul itself was little concerned with the plan, if at all (for, alas for them, they were woefully besotted, and cared chiefly for their pleasures and their lusts), Diabolus their governor was concerned. He had his spies out continually, who brought him word of everything, and they told him what was being done at court against him, and that Emmanuel would certainly come shortly with an army to invade him. Nor was there any man at court, or any peer of the kingdom, whom Diabolus feared as he feared this Prince; for, if you remember, I showed you before that Diabolus had felt the weight of his hand already. So, since it was he who was coming, Diabolus was all the more afraid.

Well, you see I have told you that the King’s Son had undertaken to come from the court to save Mansoul, and that his Father had made him Captain of the forces. The time for his setting out having now arrived, he made ready for his march, and took with him as his power five noble captains and their forces.

1. The first was that famous captain, the noble Captain Credence, whose name means faith. His were the red colors, and Mr. Promise carried them. For his escutcheon he had the holy lamb and golden shield, and he had ten thousand men at his feet.

2. The second was that famous captain, Captain Good-Hope. His were the blue colors; his standard-bearer was Mr. Expectation; for his escutcheon he had three golden anchors; and he had ten thousand men at his feet.

3. The third was that valiant captain, Captain Charity, whose name means love. His standard-bearer was Mr. Tender-heart; his were the green colors; for his escutcheon he had three naked orphans held close to the breast; and he had ten thousand men at his feet.
4. The fourth was that gallant commander, Captain Innocent. His standard-bearer was Mr. Harmless; his were the white colors; and for his escutcheon he had three golden doves.

5. The fifth was the truly loyal and well-beloved captain, Captain Patience. His standard-bearer was Mr. Suffer-Long; his were the black colors; and for his escutcheon he had three arrows through a golden heart.

These were Emmanuel’s captains; these their standard-bearers, their colors, and their escutcheons; and these the men under their command. So, as I said, the brave Prince set out on his march to the town of Mansoul. Captain Credence led the vanguard and Captain Patience brought up the rear, while the other three with their men made up the main body, the Prince himself riding in his chariot at their head.

But when they set out on their march, oh, how the trumpets sounded, how their armor glittered, and how the colors waved in the wind! The Prince’s armor was all of gold, and it shone like the sun in the sky; the captains’ armor was armor of proof, tried and true, and it looked like the glittering stars. There were also some from the court who rode along as volunteers, for the love they had for King Shaddai and for the happy deliverance of the town of Mansoul.

Emmanuel also took with him, at his Father’s command, fifty-four battering rams and twelve slings for whirling stones. Every one of these was made of pure gold, and they carried them in the heart and body of their army all the way to Mansoul.

So they marched until they came within less than a league of the town, about three miles, and there they waited until the first four captains came to brief them on how matters stood. Then they took up their journey to the town of Mansoul, and to Mansoul they came. And when the old soldiers in the camp saw that they had new forces to join them, they again gave such a shout before the walls of Mansoul that it threw Diabolus into another fright. So they sat down before the town, not as the other four captains had done, against the gates of Mansoul only, but they surrounded it on every side and beset it behind and before, so that now, whichever way Mansoul looked, it saw force and power laid in siege against it. Besides this, mounts were cast up against it: Mount Gracious on one side and Mount Justice on the other. There were also several smaller banks and forward positions, such as Plain-Truth Hill and No-Sin Banks, where many of the slings were placed against the town. Four were planted on Mount Gracious and as many on Mount Justice, and the rest were placed conveniently in various spots around the town. Five of the best battering rams, that is, the biggest of them, were placed on Mount Hearken, a mount cast up close by Ear-gate, with the intent of breaking it open.

Now when the men of the town saw the multitude of soldiers who had come up against the place, and the rams and slings, and the mounts they were planted on, along with the glittering of the armor and the waving of the colors, they were forced to shift, and shift, and shift their thoughts again; but they hardly changed them for braver thoughts, rather for fainter ones. For though before they had thought themselves well enough guarded, now they began to think that no one knew what their fate would be.

When the good Prince Emmanuel had laid siege to Mansoul in this way, he first hung out the white flag, set up among the golden slings on Mount Gracious. He did this for two reasons: first, to let Mansoul know that he could and would still be gracious if they turned to him; and second, that he might leave them all the more without excuse if he destroyed them while they continued in their rebellion.

So the white flag, with the three golden doves on it, was hung out for two whole days, to give them time and space to consider. But they, as I hinted before, as if they did not care, made no reply to the Prince’s favorable signal.

Then at his command they set the red flag on the mount called Mount Justice. It was the red flag of Captain Judgment, whose escutcheon was the burning fiery furnace; and this too stood waving before them in the wind for several days together. But they behaved under the red flag just as they had under the white; and still he took no advantage of them.

Then he had the black flag of defiance, whose escutcheon was the three burning thunderbolts, hung out against them; but Mansoul was as unconcerned at this as at the ones before it. When the Prince saw that neither mercy nor judgment, nor the carrying out of judgment, would or could come near the heart of Mansoul, he was touched with deep sorrow and said, “Surely this strange behavior of the town of Mansoul comes rather from ignorance of the customs and practices of war than from any secret defiance of us and contempt for their own lives. Or if they know the customs of war in their own country, they do not know the rites and ceremonies of the wars in which we are engaged, when I make war on my enemy Diabolus.”

So he sent to the town of Mansoul to let them know what he meant by these signs and ceremonies of the flags, and also to learn from them which they would choose: grace and mercy, or judgment and the execution of judgment. All this while they kept their gates shut with locks, bolts, and bars as fast as they could. Their guards were doubled, too, and their watch made as strong as possible. And Diabolus plucked up what courage he could to encourage the town to resist.
The townsmen answered the Prince’s messenger, in substance, as follows:
Great Sir,

As to what you have signified to us by your messenger, whether we will accept your mercy or fall by your justice: we are bound by the law and custom of this place, and can give you no definite answer. For it is against the law, the government, and the royal prerogative of our king to make either peace or war without him. But this we will do: we will petition our prince to come down to the wall, and there give you such treatment as he thinks fit and profitable for us.

When the good Prince Emmanuel heard this answer, and saw the slavery and bondage of the people, and how content they were to stay in the chains of the tyrant Diabolus, it grieved him to the heart. And indeed, whenever he saw that anyone was content under the giant’s slavery, it moved him deeply.
